directions: Sow seed directly where plants are to grow in late spring or early summer for bloom the following year, since this is a true biennial or short-lived perennial that flowers on its second-year stalk. Choose a sheltered, full-sun spot with rich, well-drained soil and stake the tall flower spikes against wind, since they can topple under their own weight once the deep maroon-black, single, saucer-shaped blooms open along the stem. Allow some seed pods to mature and drop to keep a self-sustaining stand going, since older plants often decline after flowering. Watch for hollyhock rust on the lower leaves and strip affected foliage promptly to keep the planting vigorous.

Direct sow in full sun in average, well-drained garden soil, siting plants where their tall flowering stalks will be sheltered from strong wind. This true perennial species from the Caucasus and southern Russia produces soft primrose-yellow single flowers up the length of its stem and is noticeably more resistant to hollyhock rust than common Alcea rosea, making it a better long-term choice where rust has been a problem. Once established the deep taproot resents transplanting, so choose a permanent location and divide only when necessary. Deadhead spent stalks to tidy the planting, or let a few seed heads ripen to naturalize a colony over time.

Direct sow in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this European wildflower species is a shorter, more refined cottage garden mallow than Malva sylvestris, bearing a long summer succession of pale pink or white saucer-shaped flowers above finely cut, ferny foliage that releases a faint musky scent when crushed. It thrives in poor soil and actually flops or declines in overly rich, heavily fertilized beds, so avoid excess feeding. Shear the clump back hard after the first flush of bloom to encourage a fresh round of flowers and prevent the plant from becoming leggy. It self-seeds readily, so deadhead if you want to limit its spread through the border.

Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, since this fast-growing annual mallow resents root disturbance and rarely transplants well from cell packs. This All-America Selections winning cultivar produces large, glossy, rose-pink flowers with a deeper pink throat and prominent darker veining, held above a naturally bushy, well-branched mound of soft green foliage all summer. Thin seedlings to their final spacing early, since crowded plants stretch and flop, and pinch young plants once to encourage bushier growth and more flowering side shoots. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the long summer-to-frost flowering display going strong.

Plant container-grown specimens or rooted softwood cuttings in spring into light, well-drained soil in full sun, since this fast-growing, semi-woody shrubby mallow dislikes heavy, waterlogged ground and is best propagated from cuttings rather than seed, as it does not come true. Named for the Rosemary Verey garden where it originated, it produces a long summer-to-autumn succession of large, pale blush-white flowers with a striking dark red central eye on an airy, arching shrub. Prune hard in early spring, cutting the previous year's growth back by half to two-thirds, to keep the naturally rangy shrub compact and encourage vigorous new flowering wood, since old wood becomes woody and short-lived. Watch individual branches for reversion to plain pink flowers, typical of the parent Lavatera olbia, and cut these stems out at the base to preserve the distinctive white-and-red-eyed flower color.

Direct sow on the soil surface in full sun in lean, well-drained, even gravelly soil, since this short-lived perennial mullein flowers best where it is not competing with lush neighbors or excess fertility. It forms a neat basal rosette of dark green, somewhat heart-shaped leaves and sends up slender, branched spikes of small yellow flowers distinguished by conspicuous purple hairs on the stamens, blooming over a long stretch of summer. It tolerates drought and poor soil readily once established but is short-lived, so allow some flower spikes to set seed each year to maintain a self-sustaining colony in the border or gravel garden. Cut spent flower stalks back after seed drops to tidy the planting.

Direct sow in lean, well-drained, even sandy or gravelly soil in full sun, since this compact selection of viper's bugloss flowers most intensely and stays sturdiest when grown hard, without rich soil or extra fertilizer. It forms a low, bristly mound of narrow leaves topped from early to midsummer with dense spikes of intensely gentian-blue, pink-budded flowers that are a magnet for bees. Being biennial, sow in successive years or let it self-seed to maintain continuous bloom, since first-year plants form only a rosette before flowering the following season. Its dwarf habit compared to the wild species makes it useful along the front of a sunny, dry border or in a gravel garden without staking.

Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in part shade to full shade, since this golden-leaved sport of common bear's breeches scorches badly and loses its best color in strong, direct sun. New foliage emerges a bright chartreuse-gold that deepens toward green as leaves mature, giving strong season-long color contrast in a shaded border well before the tall spikes of hooded white-and-purple flowers appear in early summer. Keep soil evenly moist through summer, since dry shade causes the thin gold leaves to brown at the edges faster than on the green-leaved species. Once established the thick, fleshy roots regenerate readily from any left-behind fragment, so site it thoughtfully and divide clumps in spring only when you are prepared to keep the resulting offsets.
